en: The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions for Quelling Disputes,
Spoken by the Buddha. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlagupta, Dharma Master of the Transmission of the Teaching, Imperially Conferred Purple Robe,
Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments and Grand Officer of the Department of State Ceremonial, under Imperial Decree, during the Western Heaven Translation Era.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the World-Honored One was staying in the village of Śāmākagrāma, observing the rains retreat (*varṣāvāsa*), while the assembly of bhikṣus, not far from the Buddha, were likewise each observing the retreat.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa named Cunda who was observing the summer retreat in the Jālūkā forest.
There, a follower of the heterodox Nigaṇṭha-putra sect, who was an extremely wicked man, suddenly passed away.
That Nirgrantha had a son who wished to engage in dispute with the śramaṇa, saying:
"The dharma and vinaya of my school are known only by me, not by you;
the dharma and vinaya of your school are known only by you, nor are they known by me."
All the dharmas I possess are entirely in accordance with reason, whereas all the dharmas you possess are entirely contrary to reason;
the harmonious dharma is mine, while the discordant dharma is yours.

Regarding all that you have said: if your former words are right, your subsequent words are wrong; if your subsequent words are right, your former words are wrong. All such speech is devoid of benefit and has nothing to be grasped; though you may speak extensively, it cannot lead to liberation, nor can it bring knowledge of the supreme, ultimate truth.
"This is what the śramaṇa has said; it does not accord with my Dharma. How could it cause me to give rise to a mind of understanding?

That Nirgrantha intentionally spoke these words to create discord, wishing to incite strife and diminish his power and capability, using the conditions of suffering and affliction to destroy the Dharma of peace and happiness.

For these reasons, wishing to give rise to unwholesome karma within the pure and white dharmas of the śramaṇa, they incite strife and various forms of destruction; giving rise to a mind of pride, they claim superiority over others, saying:

"Whatever the śramaṇas have taught is not in accordance with the Dharma or the Vinaya; it is not correctly understood and cannot lead to liberation; it does not lead toward the path to Bodhi. Your teacher is not a Tathāgata, Arhat, or Samyaksaṃbuddha."

At that time, the śramaṇa Cunda, having completed his summer retreat and finished making his robes, departed from that place; putting on his robes and taking up his bowl, he traveled by stages until he arrived at the village of Śamaka-putra.
Having arrived, he set aside his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and approached the Venerable Ānanda; bowing his head at the Venerable’s feet, he withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda asked the śramaṇa Cunda: “Cunda!
"In what place did you observe the summer retreat?
And for what reason have you come here? Cunda replied:
"Venerable Sir!
I have been observing the rains retreat in the Jālukā Grove, a place of evil omens.
There, a certain Nigaṇṭha son of the Nigaṇṭhas, who was an extremely wicked man, suddenly passed away."
The Nirgrantha had a son who wished to instigate a dispute with the śramaṇa, even going so far as to say: "Your teacher is not a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"It is for this reason that I have come here," Ānanda said to Cunda.
"Cunda! he continued.
I know this matter: because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is not present among the assembly, there are non-Buddhists who wish to incite strife and contention.

You must not engage in such disputes at this time; for if you initiate contention, it will fail to benefit many people and will instead cause many beings to give rise to various sufferings and afflictions, even extending to the hosts of devas and humans, all of whom will find no benefit and will collectively experience suffering and distress.
"Regarding the matters you have spoken of, Cunda, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, fully knows and sees them.
Let us now go together to the Buddha's presence and report these matters in detail."
Cunda replied, "Excellent, O Venerable One!
If I am granted the sight of the Buddha, I shall have attained great benefit."
Furthermore, one may hear the profound, sublime Dharma in the presence of the Buddha.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda went together with the śramaṇa Cunda to the place where the Buddha was; having arrived, they each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then the Venerable Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This śramaṇa Cunda has been observing the summer retreat in the Jālugrāma forest."
Among them was an outsider, a Nirgrantha son of Jñātiputra, who was an extremely wicked man; he suddenly passed away.
The Nirgranthas had a son who wished to incite strife against the Śramaṇa, even going so far as to say: "Your teacher is not a Tathāgata, an Arhat, or a Samyaksaṃbuddha."
For this reason, they have come to speak with me.
World-Honored One!
At that time, I said to Cunda:
"Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is not present among the assembly, there are non-Buddhists who wish to incite strife.

You must not engage in dispute at this time; if you were to start a quarrel, it would fail to benefit many people and would instead cause many beings to give rise to various sufferings, even extending to all the hosts of devas and humans, none of whom would find benefit but would all experience suffering."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"On what grounds do you say:
'The Buddha is not among the assembly, and there are groups of outsiders who have started a dispute'?"
"Is this so? Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
At one time, I saw two bhikṣus who were praised by the Buddha.
These two bhikṣus were well-versed in the Vinaya and moved with proper decorum and orderliness as they walked along together. Having seen them, I said to them:
"You two bhikṣus, you should not manifest such a manner of deportment."
When the Buddha is not among the assembly, there may be non-Buddhists who, upon seeing these signs, initiate disputes.
Once such disputes arise, they cause harm to many people, even including the hosts of devas and humans, so that none derive any benefit and all are born into suffering and affliction.
“I recall this circumstance, and therefore I spoke thus to Cūḍapanthaka.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
“What do you think?”
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am unable to fully comprehend this matter.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"I have attained manifest perfect enlightenment through my own wisdom. In the interval since then, I have extensively taught various dharmas—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path. Regarding such dharmas as these, I have fully known and fully seen all that I have proclaimed."
“Ānanda!
Many non-Buddhists are instigating disputes among the community of bhikṣus. Are you able to understand the causes of these disputes?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I am unable to know.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"It means that there may be a bhikṣu for whom the precepts sometimes increase and sometimes decrease, or for whom the deportment sometimes increases and sometimes decreases.
Ānanda! If the precepts and the deportment increase or decrease, one deviates from the constant Dharma."
Wherever he went, there were non-Buddhists who, upon seeing this, would immediately engage in strife and contention.
Once such strife arose, it caused harm to many people, even including the hosts of devas and humans, leading them all to experience suffering and affliction without any benefit.

Why is this? Ānanda! Those non-Buddhist Nirgranthas are neither omniscient nor authentic; in all places and regarding all that they perceive, everything is impure. Therefore, they constantly delight in instigating strife and contention.
"Ānanda!
You should know that when disputes arise among the community of bhikṣus, they do so because of various roots of contention.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
Excellent, Sugata!
Now is the very time; we pray that the Buddha will proclaim the root of strife, so that the bhikṣus, having heard it, may remember and uphold it, and always remain free from transgression.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Listen attentively!
Attend to it with correct mental application and remember it well; I shall now speak for you.”

Ānanda! If there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to a mind of anger and resentment, because of that anger and resentment, he does not develop a mind of reverence, respect, and so forth toward his teachers and elders, nor can he serve or make offerings to them;
because he does not revere those teachers and elders, he does not perceive the Dharma.
Because they do not perceive the Dharma, they fail to examine the community of bhikṣus correctly;
due to this incorrect examination, quarrels arise;
and because these quarrels arise, they cause harm to many people, even including the hosts of devas and humans, bringing them all suffering and distress.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who regards both the internal and the external as existing; he performs a realistic observation and applies himself with focused accumulation, yet takes delight in evil and extremely wicked mental engagements, exerts himself with perverse diligence, utters false and delusive speech, and incites strife.
Thus, with such false thoughts and lack of clear comprehension, one gives rise to what is discordant, and even fails to eradicate the conditions for strife.
Ānanda! Such matters as these are the root of strife; therefore, they give rise to all manner of suffering and affliction.

The causes of suffering and affliction refer to the initial arousal of a mind of anger and resentment, followed by the further arising of concealment, deception, guile, envy, stinginess, lack of shame and lack of dread, lack of correct awareness, adherence to views, and so forth, as well as various forms of attachment and false, deluded recollections.

Due to such various evil causes and conditions, one fails to give rise to a mind of reverence, respect, and so forth toward one's teachers and preceptors, nor is one able to serve or make offerings to them;
because of this lack of honor toward those teachers and preceptors, one does not perceive the Dharma;
and because one does not perceive the Dharma, one fails to observe correctly within the community of bhikṣus.
"Because of improper observation, disputes arise. Ānanda!
As previously stated, such conditions as these are all the roots of dispute."
For this reason, when disputes arise, there are seven methods for settling them.
As I have taught, Ānanda,
all matters of dispute— whether already arisen or not yet arisen— can be completely extinguished by these means.
What are the seven? They are:

saṃmukhavinaya (settlement in the presence), smṛtivinaya (settlement by recollection), amūḍhavinaya (settlement for one who is not insane), pratijñākāraka (settlement by confession), yadbhūyaiṣīya (settlement by the majority), tasya pāpeyaśika (settlement by acknowledging what has been done), and tṛṇaprastāraka (settlement like covering with grass);
these are the seven kinds.
"What is called the method for settling disputes through *saṃmukhavinaya*?

Ānanda, it refers to one person teaching the Dharma and Vinaya to another; one person teaching two people; one person teaching many people; and one person teaching the great assembly—thus, the four types of 'presence' (*saṃmukha*) are established."

Two people expound the Dharma and Vinaya for one person; two people expound for one, two people expound for many, and two people expound for the great assembly—thus four cases are established in the presence [of the Sangha].

Many people expound the Dharma and Vinaya for one person; many people expound for two, many people expound for many, and many people expound for the great assembly—thus four cases are established in the presence [of the Sangha].

The great assembly expounds the Dharma and Vinaya for one person; the great assembly expounds for two, the great assembly expounds for many, and the great assembly expounds for the great assembly—thus four cases are established in the presence [of the Sangha].
This is called the legal procedure for settling disputes through *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of).
By means of this method, contentious matters can be brought to an end.
What is called the legal procedure for settling disputes through *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection)?
Ānanda! Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, having committed an offense, does not recall it himself. Other bhikṣus say to him:
"You have committed this offense; you ought to recall it and seek compassion from the assembly to obtain the *smṛtivinaya* (the legal procedure for restoration through recollection)."
That bhikṣu then entered the assembly and sought compassion from the great multitude, requesting that the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) be granted to him.
At that time, the great assembly, following the instruction of the Great Teacher, granted him the *smṛtivinaya*.
Once this bhikṣu has been cleared of the offense, the dispute is extinguished.
This is called the method for settling disputes through the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection).
By means of this method, the dispute is able to be extinguished.
"What is called the method for settling disputes through the *amūḷhavinaya* (the discipline of non-delusion)?

Ānanda, it refers to a case where a bhikṣu, being deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or tormented by intense pain, is unable to practice in accordance with the Dharma despite his great learning; he even misrepresents the teachings he has heard as mere confused chatter. Having spoken thus, he departs from the community."
When that bhikṣu later regains his original mind, the other bhikṣus shall say to him:
"You have committed this offense; you must enter the assembly and beg the great multitude for mercy, performing the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the disciplinary procedure for one who was not insane)."
That bhikṣu then entered the assembly and sought compassion from the great multitude, requesting the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the disciplinary procedure for one who was not insane).
At that time, the great multitude, following the instructions of the Great Teacher, granted him the *amūḍha-vinaya*.
Once this bhikṣu has been cleared of the offense, the dispute is extinguished.
This is called the method for settling disputes through the *amūḷhavinaya* (the verdict of sanity).
By means of this method, the matter of dispute can be brought to an end.
"What is called the legal procedure for settling disputes through confession (*pātimokkha-thapanā*)?

Ānanda, it refers to when a bhikṣu, being ignorant of the characteristics of an offense, claims to know and understand them extensively, and then makes such a statement before the assembly: [text continues]"
"Venerable One!
It is because gain and offerings are difficult for me to obtain.
The other bhikṣus said to him:

"You do not know or understand the characteristics of this offense, yet you claim to know and understand them extensively. You have committed this offense; you must now seek the compassion of the assembly and repent for your transgression."
That bhikṣu then entered the midst of the assembly and, seeking the compassion of the great multitude, repented and reproached himself.
At that time, the great assembly, following the instructions of the Great Teacher, granted him the *svavacanadaṇḍakarma* (the disciplinary act of confession).
Once this bhikṣu has been cleared of the offense, the dispute is extinguished.
This is called the method for extinguishing disputes through confession (*pāpadeśanā*).
By means of this method, the dispute is able to be brought to an end.
"What is called the method for settling disputes by means of a majority vote?

Ānanda, it refers to when two bhikṣus living in the same residence suddenly engage in a dispute, giving rise to various kinds of speech and extensively provoking contention; each adheres to his own position, one saying it is the Dharma and the other saying it is not the Dharma, one saying it is the Vinaya and the other saying it is not the Vinaya, one saying it is an offense and the other saying it is not an offense."
If these two bhikṣus can settle their dispute when it arises, that is well.
If they do not settle it, these two bhikṣus will leave their original residence and raise the dispute in another location.
Once they have departed from that place, it would be well if they were able to settle the dispute along the way.
If they do not settle it, then a large community of bhikṣus shall collectively resolve the dispute:
some shall explain it by means of the Sūtras, some by means of the Vinaya, and some by means of the Mātṛkās.
Because he explained it in detail for the sake of many people, the dispute between these two bhikṣus was extinguished.
This is called the method for settling disputes through the majority opinion.
By means of this method, one is able to cause disputes to be pacified and extinguished.
"What is called the method for settling disputes by knowing what has been done? Ānanda!"

That is to say, if a bhikṣu, having committed an offense, recognizes that he has transgressed—whether he has spoken of it to others or not—and after reflecting upon it himself, goes to another bhikṣu, removes his leather sandals, bares one shoulder before the bhikṣu, places his right knee on the ground, and three times declares his own name and clan:
"I have committed this offense and dare not conceal it; I come before the Venerable One to seek compassionate confession."
"I only pray that the Venerable One will grant me the joy of absolution.
Then that Venerable One immediately accepted the confession.
Once that bhikṣu had attained purity, the Venerable One said:
"Do you see these signs of transgression?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I have already seen these signs of transgression."
The Venerable One spoke again:
"You should uphold the code of discipline in accordance with the Dharma.
The Bhikṣu replied:
"I now duly uphold the code of discipline.
Thus he says three times.
This is called the method for settling disputes by means of acknowledging what has been done.
By means of this method, one is able to cause disputes to be pacified.
"What is called the method for settling disputes by covering them over with grass, Ānanda? [It is as follows:]..."
It refers to when a community of bhikṣus gathers in one place and, having engaged in mutual strife, divides into two factions.
At that time, within one faction, those who are elders stay together, those who know the Dharma stay together, and those who are leaders stay together.
Thereupon, among the group there was a bhikṣu who, for the sake of gain and offerings, initiated a dispute.
Having initiated this dispute, he spoke thus within his own assembly:
"In such-and-such a place, lay followers find it easy to obtain gain and offerings; I shall speak according to the Dharma and Vinaya in their midst."
There are other bhikṣus who, for this reason, have initiated a dispute against me.
Venerable sirs!

If I have committed an offense of dispute on account of this matter, I pray that the venerable ones will relinquish this offense of mine; even my intentional entering of the houses of laypeople shall all be permitted to be confessed and removed, as it constitutes the commission of a duṣkṛta offense.
From this day forward, I shall not commit such acts; should I ever do so again, I shall seek compassion and repent before the Venerable Ones, for I dare not conceal whatever I have done.
While that bhikṣu was performing this confession, a single bhikṣu within his own faction did not grant permission for the confession.

Thereupon, that bhikṣu entered the other faction; he removed his leather sandals, bared one shoulder, and after having paid his respects in order to the senior elders, he returned before the presiding elder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and stood there, addressing the assembly:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"In such-and-such a place, it is easy to obtain requisites for the white-robed lay followers; there, I shall speak according to the Dharma and Vinaya.
For this reason, other bhikṣus have raised a dispute against me."

I then sought confession according to the Dharma within my own assembly; however, at that time, there was one bhikṣu in my assembly who would not grant me absolution. Therefore, I have come here to seek your compassionate forgiveness.
Venerable sirs!

If I have committed an offense of contention on account of this matter, may the venerable sirs relinquish this offense of mine; even as I depart from the house of a layperson, may you all permit me to perform confession, for I have committed an offense of *duṣkṛta*.
I now seek compassionate forgiveness before all the virtuous ones; whatever I have done, I dare not conceal. May the virtuous ones grant me permission to repent and bestow upon me their joy.
At that time, the great assembly granted permission for the confession.
Once that bhikṣu had attained purification, the elder addressed him, saying:
"Do you recognize this characteristic of the offense?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“I have already recognized these signs of transgression.
The elder spoke again:
"You should uphold the discipline in accordance with the Dharma.
The bhikṣu replied,
"I shall now uphold the discipline in accordance with the Dharma."
Thus he spoke three times.

At that time, among the other faction, those who were elders gathered in one place; those who were knowers of the Dharma gathered in one place; and those who were leaders gathered in one place, just as in this faction.
Thereupon, among the group, there was a bhikṣu who, for the sake of gain and offerings, initiated a dispute.
Having initiated the dispute, he spoke thus within his own assembly:
"A certain layperson’s gains and offerings are easy to obtain; I shall speak according to the Dharma and Vinaya regarding him."
"Other bhikṣus, on account of this matter, gave rise to disputes.
Thus it continued, with the second and third rounds of questioning and answering, as explained in detail previously.

Ānanda! When those various bhikṣus have recognized their own transgressions and gone to confess them through mutual exchange, they greet one another with respect when they meet; they extinguish the conditions for dispute, cease all idle talk, and no longer give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding even the slightest phenomenon.
This is called the method for settling disputes by covering them over with grass.
By means of this method, contentious matters can be brought to an end. Ānanda!
“Monks, you should all remember these seven methods for settling disputes.
Furthermore, Ānanda,
there are six kinds of dharmas for concord and respect.”

Listen attentively, apply your minds correctly, and bear this well in mind; I shall now speak for you. What are these six? They are as follows: practicing acts of loving-kindness through bodily action;

constantly cultivating the pure conduct of celibacy in the presence of the Buddha; honoring, revering, and practicing the true Dharma according to principle; and dwelling in harmony with the community of bhikṣus. These are called the dharmas of concordant respect regarding bodily action.
Furthermore, regarding verbal action, one utters words of loving-kindness and harmony, free from all conflict and contention; this is called the dharma of harmonious respect in verbal action.

Furthermore, regarding mental action, one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness and harmony, without any opposition or contrariness; this is called the dharma of harmonious respect in mental action.

Furthermore, whatever spiritual benefits or worldly gains one obtains should be shared equally with all who receive them. At times, when one goes on almsround with the bowl in sequence, whatever food or other items are obtained should be announced to the community so that they may know; these should be received together with the community and not used privately or in secret. If the community is made aware of this, it constitutes the practice of the holy life (*brahmacarya*); this is called the Dharma of Harmonious Respect.

Furthermore, when one’s precepts are neither broken nor interrupted, and through the power of those precepts one has become firm, stainless, and pure; when one knows the proper time and place with universal equanimity, and is worthy of receiving the offerings of food and drink from donors; and when such pure precepts are practiced together, understood together, and used to cultivate the holy life together—this is called the Dharma of Reverent Harmony in Precepts.

Furthermore, if one sees that noble wisdom leads to the realization of the path of deliverance, even unto the ultimate end of suffering, and having seen such characteristics as they truly are, one acts in concert, understands in concert, and practices the holy life in concert—this is called the Dharma of concord through mutual respect.
These and others like them are called the six dharmas of harmonious respect. "Ānanda!

Regarding the roots of strife previously mentioned, you bhikṣus should sever and eliminate them. You should thoroughly understand the seven methods for settling disputes, so that all matters of contention—whether already arisen or not yet arisen—are entirely extinguished, and you may together cultivate the six dharmas of harmonious respect."

"O Bhikṣus! If you practice in this manner, then wherever you go—in the east, west, south, or north—whether walking or staying, it shall bring peace and happiness to all of you bhikṣus, and free you from all disputes.

Even after my parinirvāṇa, it shall likewise ensure that you, the community of bhikṣus, always attain peace and happiness in all places, no different from when I am currently dwelling in the world, teaching the Dharma, and transforming sentient beings."
The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions for Settling Disputes Spoken by the Buddha.
